p: Thank you. I did have one follow up question and then I’ll turn it over to Council Member Brewer. So, you mentioned that some of the roles require 16 week training. Is that for PEP Officers and Rangers? So, how do you deal with retention if 3 months out of the 12 months that you know these roles are I guess essentially affected to the one shots come up again. How do you deal with retention? That has to be difficult.
Yeah, that’s a great question. You know in general, retention for PEP has been like a big priority of ours and an ongoing -
16 weeks, that’s four months.
Four months.
Wow, okay.

It’s a great question. In general I’d say retention for PEP has been an ongoing conversation within our agency for some time and let me just start out by saying that I’m so incredibly grateful for this incredibly talented workforce.

They have extremely difficult jobs. You know and they are trained peace keepers. They are there to educate but truly, oftentimes as I am sure anyone would know around PEP, their jobs are to enforce rules. To tell people to make sure that they’re not allowed to park in parkland. That they need to get their dogs on a leash and out of the flowerbeds. That they need to adhere to our rules, not throw garbage on the ground. Really follow the rules that we have in place and that is extremely tough. So, I think that you know it has been difficult in terms of retention. We saw at some point a loss of around 25 percent per year, which was very, very concerning. I do want to give a huge shoutout to our leadership, particularly our Deputy Commissioner Margaret Nelson, our Assistant Commissioner Asha Harris, whom I’m sure many people have met with here because she’s so good and such a wonderful advocate for her unit. But we have been through kind of a dedicated campaign to really remove this notion of PEP as a stepping stone and really remind folks that this can be a true career but this is - this doesn’t have to be a stepping stone to NYPD or Corrections or any other kind of unit that you can have a very satisfying

career in PEP. That’s been accomplished through uhm, kind of a very proactive campaign and really kind of robust recruitment. That’s more than just kind of sitting at job fairs and having anybody who kind of comes by to fill out an application. We’re really trying to explain to folks the benefits of this job and what they are signing on for at the very, very beginning and we’ve seen that that retention rate has increased. We now see a much lower attrition rate around 15 percent in comparison to the last two years and that’s in large part thanks to the efforts of the agency.
So, you mentioned that many of them you know go to PD or Corrections. Have you considered offering pay parity to those agencies uh, with the PEP Officers?

It’s a good question. Again, I don’t - I’m unable to speak to the kind of uh, uh, pay that these other agencies are providing to their staff but we’re happy to look into this and get back to you more, further. You know we’ve also been though I will say, trying to break this idea and this narrative of this is like the natural way or this is the same thing or you are essentially NYPD for Parks.

Because that’s not true. We really rely on a good partnership with the NYPD to deal with serious crime in the entirety of the city, not just in parks but everywhere. Uh, what our PEP officers are doing is really different. They are peace keepers. They are there to really provide education first. They are there really to protect our patrons, all of them. Care holistically for everybody who comes into our parks. Also protect the parks themselves. It’s a kind of different thing and so we’re you know while we’re happy to look at those kind of pay scales and certainly, I don’t have the information in front of me. I can’t speak to other agencies. I will say that we’re also trying to break this notion of this being like the same thing but just in parks. We really want our officers to feel pride in being parks enforcement patrol and letting that stand on its own without feeling the need to compare to Corrections or
Thank you. Council Member Gale Brewer.

Alright, thank you. I just want to thank the staff for something. One is, there’s a lot of hate messages on benches and rocks.

Mostly antisemitism and to the credit of your staff, they call PD. You know the process. They take the photo and then parks renews it. But it happens weekly, so I just want to thank the staff for that. Okay, so I have a long list. Number one, water fountains, 63 percent don’t work. So, how are you dealing with water fountains that don’t work across the city? Number two, great to have new bathrooms but what about the bathrooms in my parks that are probably preserved for landmarking and need to have the kind of $13- to $5 million retention and renovation. That’s number 1,2, 3- trees. I hate that program. So, my question would be we have a bill that’s going to be introduced to have a parallel program. So, do you have a list of all the vacant tree pits, stumps? Is that on your map? I think your map is just new trees. So, that program, we can’t wait 9 years. I got people calling me everyday and so, I’d like to know if you have some suggestions of what it would cost to have a parallel program? You can do this neighborhood thing, whatever the hell it is but I want to see something in between. How often are

parks cleaned? We have the FIFA people coming, the sailing people coming, the visitors hopefully on a grand scale. They’ll hopefully be in the parks and my experience is Sunday night and Sunday night is a bad situation. So, I want to know, are parks cleaned 7 days a week or is it 5 days a week? I think it’s 5 days a week. We know that may not come till next year but the jail program didn’t work great in terms of getting rid of the snow in the school yard. So, I just want to know how that’s going to take place next year. The news stands at West 72nd Street, I guess they’re just like the one here. We’d like to see one go with something. I think the flower man is supposed to come. I don’t know what happened to the flower man. And then the other one is vacant. So, again, revenue and finally ones in the Hudson wants to know what happened to their I guess electrical issue and also, we want the stage which they don’t have this year. They need it back.
Okay great. Okay, I’m going to try and get - I think I got you on most of these. Okay, okay, uh, water fountains. None should be on right now because it’s so early.
I know but they didn’t work last year.

We’re happy to look into this. I think that I saw the list particularly because I was a Manhattan BC, so I saw- I think the list was mostly reflective of water fountains that were in Central Park. We work very closely with our -
Riverside also.

Oh, in Riverside but we work very closely with our conservancy partners and happily be kind of proactively looking at this but nobody should have water fountains right now. Everybody should be having water fountains in just a couple weeks from now because even if it’s warming up, it’s not time. We’ll be following up there but we hear you and we’re very, we’re typically pretty much on it and our entire team in terms of plumbers will be doing this work. Thousands of water fountains will be being turned on in just a couple weeks time. When it comes to renovations and PRB’s, yes, very aware of definitely really high ticket ones particularly in your district and you know this but it’s just worth repeating that when we talk about

PRB’s, there is your standard 20 by 20 and then there’s something like a dinosaur playground in Riverside which is just kind of beyond in terms of landmarks, in terms of the staff space. In terms of the fact that it’s retaining wall and it’s got stairs associated with it. It’s built into a wall. All of these complications are extremely frustrating, very important, very unique but also mean that just a higher ticket price and a higher kind of overall price tag. Not that it should be impossible but certainly has - we’ve been kind of in regular conversation with again, the Riverside Park Conservancy and others around ways that we can try to address this in a faster way. Uhm, when it comes to trees, uh and tree pit map, I don’t believe that we have this but I do think that this is why in part we - this is again, I know you don’t care for the 9 year program, but it is our way of being - our timeline right now to be able to assess every single sidewalk.
But we have hundreds of vacant trees, hundreds. That’s not going to work.
Yeah uhm-
9 years, that’s not going to work.
Yeah, I definitely hear -
We’re going to do legislation to try to come up with something else, just so you know. I hope my colleagues sign on.

Great, uhm, but we’re happy to get back in terms of any of the other data around your district and trees. Parks are cleaned 7 days a week. Parks are cleaned 7 days a week and parks are cleaned at a minimum, we have staff and particularly in your district, we have staff because your parks are often opened and closed. We have staff who are opening them, doing an -
I’m talking about the big parks, not the community parks, the big parks. Riverside is cleaned 7 days a week?

Yes, and I’ll look - yes, yes. So, it’s clean and on top of that, we have our second shift staff which are also in both Riverside Park and others that provide an additional layer of cleaning on top of park circling 7 days a week. We do - JOP is built into our snow, winter weather -
But they were not cleaned this year. That’s a fact.

It’s definitely secondary to perimeter sidewalks. So, first and foremost, we hit those perimeter sidewalks. First and foremost, we hit those major transit hubs and then we go to JOP’s. Happy to look into this closer but that is definitely our kind of prioritization.
The kids were not able to play in the yards.
Okay and then in terms of the revenue for 72nd Street, we’re happy to look into this further but I think that that concession spot in general has been discussed and we’re actively -
They’re vacant right now? You would think you would want some revenue for them.
Absolutely.
Okay and my drums on the Hudson. What about their stage?
So, I’m happy to look into this more.
They’ve always had one. They didn’t get it this year.

Yeah, this is a good question for just - we do have limited access to Wagner Wagons and this policy has been adjusted in the last year or so. So, typically, uh because this is and just be very clear, we start to look at how groups in Manhattan were having access to Wagner Wagons versus groups in Queens, versus groups in Brooklyn and realizing that the rules were not the same based on the borough, which is not great.
This group has had it for years. It brings in Native Americans from all over the country. So, I hope that it can be reconsidered for this particular one.

We definitely have a policy in place. I’m not sure if they’re in adherence with that but we’re happy to talk to them. We’re also happy to direct them towards other alternatives if for whatever reason it doesn’t comply but we know Drums on the Hudson really well. We’ve worked with them, so.
They’re calling me everyday.
Okay, well we can certainly follow up with them.
Thank you.
Yeah.
Alright, we’ve been joined by Majority Whip Kamillah Hanks who does have one question and then we’re going to Brooklyn to Council Member Sandy Nurse.
Thank you Chair because now we’re going to Staten Island.
The borough of parks.

The borough of parks. Thank you so much and it’s good to see you Commissioner. One quick question, so parks is responsible for planting trees in front of uhm, particularly in Staten Island in front of homeowners houses, residents. Uhm, often homeowners wake up and they see a tree planted and they’re like wow this is great and then, the tree grows, concrete is broken and then possibly it is DOT’s issue but then, so my question is, how are we going to work with residents of the City of New York when of course, you know trees are life? We love them but how are we going to mitigate some of the sidewalk damage and is there an avenue for residents to say hey, I don’t want a tree. Thank you.

Thank you for the question and it’s good to see you. You know to be very honest with you, this if often times where we can see some conflicts arise because we see of course, it’s our responsibility to both increase the amount of tree canopy but also, ensure that every single neighborhood benefits from the - from what trees can provide, particularly shade, particularly resiliency, water kind of retention from storms.

And one more thing to add, so Staten Island homes love their solar panels because that is one way we can be environmentally you know conscious and those trees can harm them from doing that, so we just add that in.

Yeah, and you know as in any part of New York City, it’s pretty common to see infrastructure butting up against other infrastructure, be it solar panels or sewage underneath the ground or electrical or things, or streets and sidewalks. So, it is - you know I kind of believe in just embracing the conflict there and understanding that all of these pieces of infrastructure have a role. They are all incredibly important, inclusive of trees and we have to find the

best way to kind of coexist with all of this infrastructure. So, uhm, you know one thing is I would really love to make sure that your constituents know and can anticipate when a tree is getting planted. We should have no surprises to the extent possible. I don’t want them to wake up one day and just realize that a tree is there. I would like them to know beforehand. We want to make sure that you know beforehand, that the Community Board knows beforehand that they can be excited about additional infrastructure coming in. So, one is just trying to manage everybody's expectations and have them understand what we’re trying to do and what we’re trying to accomplish. The second is that, when those trees eventually grow and we hope that they do, uh and we are - we do have a mandate and are trying to plant in every plantable street in New York City. So, that does mean that you know we are looking to do it regardless of maybe an individual homeowner's desire not to see one. Our kind of mandate and goal here is to plant everywhere where we can. Ultimately with the idea of cooling down our entire city of like trying to take away some of that extra water, of trying to serve everybody as

the city as a whole. But I want to do so as considerate uh, like with the community in mind and being as considerate and as communicative as possible. Uhm, and when eventually you see trees uprooting sidewalks or trees coming into conflict with other pieces of infrastructure. Then you know we are also there to help provide either support or guidance in the next steps that can be taken. So, there are some programs for - there are some programs for single family homes where parks can take on that responsibility to making those repairs but we’re also happy if that’s not the case. If there’s a different - if there is a different situation where they’re not eligible for that program, then we can provide additional guidance on the repairs that need to be - that need to happen as well.

And if I can just add, since you mentioned mitigation, that our forestry division has actually taken a close look at its planting strategies over the years. And as best practices have evolved, so wider tree pits, choosing species that will hopefully lead to less conflicts over time. Like our teams are constantly updating their

strategies and we’ve seen a lot of progress on that front.
Yeah, we don’t want to plant trees that have roots that are so evasive and so you know we can plant - we can have a tree there but it doesn’t have to be a maple tree that - whose roots is uprooting.
We want to maximize the benefits in terms of its canopy while minimizing the conflict, sure.
Thank you so much Chair.
Uh, we’re going to Brooklyn, Council Member Sandy Nurse.
Am I the first Brooklyn? Maybe?
No.

Okay, fine. I just have one question. Uhm, we’ve always and because I spoke with you this weekend and I asked questions last, uh hearing and everyone has asked a ton of questions. I don’t have anything else except for my district. Uhm, we’ve benefitted from a second shift at Highland Park the last two summers. Can you confirm if that’s still on for this summer and I believe for Cityline

Park also we might have had additional support. So, I just want to get confirmation of those two.

Yeah, so, looking at our Acting First Deputy Commissioner who is uh, you’re welcome to come up and answer but it sounds like uh, it sounds like the answer is yes. But before he gives you that confirmation and hopefully he can, what I just want to say is that you know with second shift, we’re very excited to have enough staff to fill our 200 different parks, I believe. And, and so, we really do so using a sort of data driven approach. We want to make sure that the staff are put in parks where we see the most activity so that we can kind of address the most pressing needs but with that being said, I’m pretty sure that these two sites are included in that. Go ahead Commissioner.

Thank you. Please raise your right hand if you’re able. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this Committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?

I do. Council Member, thank you for your question. Bottom line, yes. Uhm, both sites are - all of our second shift staff are

baselined versus one shot, which is a lot of conversation here.
Right.
They’re baselined and they’re permanently located. So, they are year round. So, in both of the parks, you mentioned Cityline and Highland, they are not just seasonally, they are there year round.
Okay, that’s great. Uhm, and then I do have one more question. Uhm, I don’t know - are you familiar with what’s happening at the Bushwick City Farm?
No, I’m sorry, please let me hear more.

And I’m just raising it here because there are some folks here who probably will testify about it later on. But the Bushwick City Farm just south of Broadway has been around for a very, very long time. Uhm, huge community asset, lots of food growing. They were also incredibly supportive during the influx of asylum seekers and supporting a lot of the folks in a temporary housing situation there. I believe recently DOB has come in and maybe issued some threats about evictions because

of like a shed or something that’s been there for years. So, really hoping that you all can have conversations with DOB to resolve this so we can keep this so we can keep this really beautiful community asset here.

Sure so let me just say and of course, I just said that I’m not too familiar with this but we’re happy to look into this more. In general, our Green Thumb Gardens should have a very close relationship with Parks staff. I love our staff that does the green thumb work. Green thumbs are very important. They provided a different way for people to connect with the soil, the land, to advocate for their communities and care for their communities, as you just said to reflect the kind of diversity that’s in their community. So, it’s a very important kind of portfolio piece and we’re happy to look into this a little bit more and certainly, at the very least, I want to make sure that the folks who are a part of this Green Thumb Garden don’t feel that they have to wait for a public hearing or something like that to get our attention on this. They should be able to kind of work with us directly all the time, so that they know that we’re -

And to be clear and sorry, I don’t have all the information in front of me but I’m not sure if it’s specifically Green Thumb Garden or not but it is a garden space and it has been there for a very long time. Even if it’s not, uhm, it’s a well established part community garden and I'm seeing the head shaking so I’m like, I get what you’re about to say.
Yeah.

But even when we have uhm gardens that have emerged and have really taken root, you know I think parks has a role to play in helping to support those places stay established regardless of whatever the status is. Because especially when it’s been there for a very long time and so integrated into the community.

Yeah, I’ll just add, like to the notion, my understanding is that it’s right, so i don’t believe it’s on like Parks jurisdiction but having said that, our Green Thumb team has hundred- there are hundreds of gardens that fit under the rubric that aren’t on our -but they are either registered with us or we provide services or guidance, and so, I’m sure happy to look into this

and help wherever we can in terms of - you know because obviously it’s a key community asset.
Okay, thank you very much. Thank you Chair.
No problem and I stand corrected. You were the first from Brooklyn to ask questions. Thank you from Brooklyn. We’re going back to the Borough of Parks Council Member Morano.

Thank you Chair. As the Chair pointed out, I do represent the Borough of Parks proudly. The issue of tree restitution is something that gets talked about a great deal when it comes to housing but a lot of folks aren’t aware of the Parks Departments role when it comes to tree restitution, including the fact that they need to pay the city when there’s park construction, either for park or addition of park. I’m wondering if you could mention - a lot of people think that maybe we should just exempt the Parks Department from paying tree restitution but I’m wondering if you can talk about that concept generally and how much the Parks Department pays specifically when it comes to tree restitution.

Sure, thank you so much for the question and I’ll look to our Assistant Commissioner for Forestry to come up and just give a little bit more details but let me just - so when we talk about tree restitution, we talk about like what happens when we have to remove - when anybody has to remove a living, healthy tree. And this happens sometimes for housing purposes. They want to build. This happens often times we may say you have to put in a new tree. If you’re building more than I think 25 feet of space on like a city block, then it’s expected to put in a new tree but also it can happen with our own projects. You’ll see many projects being designed that will show you a new design. We try to avoid it at all costs because yes, even the Parks Department is beholden towards kind of that tree restitution piece. We, you know, if you are the Borough of Parks, we’re the agency of trees.
Department of trees, sure.

And so, it’s uhm, who else but the parks department would be there to try to defend and protect our existing tree canopy. Uh, to the fullest extent possible and there are some pretty

hefty fees and kind of costs associated with taking out a healthy tree because as you heard from Council Member, our last hearing on the subject, when it comes to canopy, even though we’re very happy about planting new trees, it’s those existing trees, the maintenance of those existing trees. The maintenance of the existing canopy. That’s really what’s going to get us that shade. That’s really what’s going to get us that canopy in our lifetimes is really that existing kind of trees that we have in place. So, I’ll let our Assistant Commissioner Ben Osborne talk a little bit more specifically about the cost associated with it but it is a kind of portion of our responsibilities that we take very seriously.
Mmm, mmm.

Thank you. Please raise your right hand if you’re able. Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your testimony before this Committee and to respond honestly to Council Member questions?
Yes, I do.
Thank you.

Good afternoon Council Member. Thank you for the question. So, uhm, yes, as the

Commissioner said, you know Parks mandate includes the preservation of existing trees wherever possible, wherever appropriate and that is consistent with the legislation that the Council passed in 2023 for the city to increase the canopy cover across all jurisdictions to 30 percent and you know as the Commissioner mentioned, the vast majority of the canopy increase that we have seen in recent years, 90 percent of that is from the growth of existing trees. So, preserving existing trees wherever appropriate, really is essential to meeting the city’s goals. Now, of course, we know that there are times when trees need to be removed. Uhm, so and our policies do allow for us to permit the removal of healthy trees when there is an unavoidable conflict with the construction project. Whether that’s a residential project. Whether that’s park construction or another agency, the same laws and rules apply to any entity who may need to remove a tree. Uhm, so just a little bit on terminology, when we’re talking about the removal of permitted trees, uhm, we kind of speak about that as far as tree replacement. Uhm, restitution tends to be used to

speak about fines for illegal activities, damage, or destruction of trees. The council did pass legislation in 2021 limiting the value of permitted tree removals in residential districts R1 through R3. So, for the development of those smaller homes or any other work that takes place in those lower density residential districts. Uh, the replacement of those permanent removals is capped at twice the caliber value of trees. So, I’m happy to do a deeper dive at some point about how we do those calculations but it’s significantly lower in those lower density residential districts.
Do you know how much Parks pays?
Well, parks in terms of the parks capital project, when we’re removing trees on our own property?
Right.

I don’t have those dollar values in front of me but just as far as the policy, uhm, so the objective of the law and our own rules and internal policies is to replace the trees. It’s not necessarily the dollars. So, if we’re removing trees in a park, we first start by planting trees right

back in that park. Any balance that cannot be met within that park would be moved typically from the project of that capital - the budget of that capital project to our tree planting project budget and we can get you those dollars.

That would be great. Thank you. I’m going to take advantage that the Chair stepped out for a second and ask you a couple more quick questions. Uh, Staten Island- Commissioner, as you know, Staten Island has just one Deputy Chief of Operations, while every other borough has two. Given that your own testimony emphasizes equity and fairness, how do you justify - not you but how does one justify that imbalance and do you think it would be wise to bring Staten Island to parity with the rest of the city?

Yeah, thank you so much for the question. So, uh, and well done on the knowledge of the staffing with Staten Island. Very impressive. Uhm, so you know what I would say is that you know we are looking at it’s not just looking at every single borough to just make sure that they had the exact amount but we really are looking at - we take a data

driven approach. We look at our PIP ratings, our Parks Inspection report ratings to make sure that - to see where we stand. To see where we’re hurting in terms of maintenance. I spoke to the Council Member uh from Brooklyn just a couple weeks ago about wanting to make sure that for her constituents that live in Brooklyn, they should not have a vastly different experience at their parks and the cleanliness of their parks in Brooklyn than they do in Queens. For Staten Island, Staten Island has a really good picture right now of overall incredible PIP ratings. I can tell you when I was the Manhattan Borough Commissioner, I used to hate going behind Staten Island in terms of our reports because there would always be a dip compared to what’s happening in Staten Island but you’re also right, there are some pieces to the maintenance and operations plan that we are keenly aware of when it comes to making sure that the team in Staten Island has what they need in order to again carry out their responsibilities. We’re kind of in constant communication particularly with this Administration and all our colleagues at OMB to try to make sure that we’re continuously advocating

for what Staten Island needs to continue to have high ratings, high performing parks. Then also make sure that the rest of the city is also getting the support that they need. But we do use a data driven approach. Staten Island’s data is very strong. It does currently - they do currently have one Deputy Chief of Operations. You know we’re always happy to kind of look at this closer to make sure that - that staffing does not impact kind of their overall -

So, the engine though, Staten Island has the most park land per capita in the city, right? And so, and we’re proud of that, that’s why we’re the Borough of the Parks. In general, do you think we’re receiving staffing and maintenance resources proportional to that responsibility or are we being asked to do more with less?

Yeah, it’s not, thank you for the question and I appreciate the advocacy. It’s really not just the amount of park space per capita. We really look at overall usage. We look at overall kind of popular - like where we see most New Yorkers gathering. We still get our PIP ratings, which again are like our secret shopper program that is

completely neutral to see where are we performing highest? Where are the most folks going? What - like overall looking at that picture. Of course, how much ground are our staff covering and how much are we responsible for? Where are we seeing additional support? So, and so, with - with all of that bigger picture in mind, we make our staffing decisions. Ultimately, I think that given Staten Island’s consistently high ratings, we’re happy with that but we also, trust me when I tell you that and I just came from Fresh Kills just yesterday. I was spending the day out there with my kids. I was just at South Beach, just two weekends prior to there, walking along the boardwalk, looking at the boardwalk there to think about what can be done in the future. It is - I certainly don’t want anybody in Staten Island to think that they are secondary to any other portion of this portfolio that is parks. They are a very important borough to me. The park land over there is incredibly important to make sure that we upkeep to the highest degree possible.
Thank you and the next time you’re on Staten Island, I hope you’ll let me know so I can show you some of my favorite parts.
You got to tell me some food places to go, I was looking around.
You just let me know the next time you are there and you will not be disappointed.
Okay.
Thank you Commissioner.
Yeah.

Alright, uhm, I know I stepped out for a second. I’m going to go back to Brooklyn, yes. Uh, Council Member Narcisse and Deputy Leader Banks. Uhm, for the sake of - we can give them an additional two minutes, each to their time clocks, so 7 minutes each.

Thank you Chair but Staten Island took 20 minutes, so I’m going to take 30 because we’re the best part of the City of New York. Uhm, Commissioner, again, congratulations. I appreciate you so much. I have to go to the best part of New York City but I have to stay here because there’s Booklyn in the house, so we have to ask the question because I have the pleasure to represent one part of the New York City that have a lot of parks.

And thank you to all your leadership because I love parks. Uhm, I don’t know if you know, we fought very hard to get that $1 billion but we did not but God knows we probably will get - it’s probably before we leave here. Uhm, so, thank you for all the work you’re doing. I’m looking at uhm, the lifeguards. I wish I could have some in my district. I’m helping to hire but I don’t have no place to give them. We don’t have no swimming pool, except the beach, so I hope we’re looking at to how we can get swimming pool equity around New York City but the prior speaker worked very hard for that and congratulations Shirley Chisholm. I know my colleague Farah Louis, worked very hard to get that and yes, go like this for her. She worked very hard to get it and I’m looking forward to have one before I go even. I will not cut the ribbon, but I would like to see it happening. Marine Park Playground, I know one of my colleagues that’s talking about it. Six years in the making for the playground. The families are getting to me every single day. Uhm, I hope we can do something about it. So, for me, what the delay is so bad. 6 years in the making, fully funded. That’s

not acceptable and it’s a playground for the children. That became a safety issue. So, I’m going to leave it to them. So, we have a few - because I have some of my colleagues in the house that really help me, NYC H2O, thank you and all the organizations that are doing amazing things. To follow up with the Chair question about Park Department salaries. The average salary for a New York City Parks gardener is $55,000. The gardener at Tompkins Square Park hasn’t been filled in 2 years. How many gardener positions need to be filled?

Thank you so much for your questions and for your partnership and advocacy. It was really good to see you at Shirley Chisholm, a couple times I think and uh I also look forward to talking to you about certainly about additional funding for either pools or just also just access to the water for your constituents. It is incredibly important. We know that what parks is doing is teaching lifesaving skills that completely change the game, change outcomes for constituents and it is very important work. So, I would love to continue to partner with you on thinking through what that looks like.

When it comes to Marine Park, I want to tell you that when I was in Fresh Kills yesterday but also took my kids to Marine Park. They loved it so much. We wanted to see for ourselves the playground project and I wanted to take a walk around there. So, I definitely hear you, it is far time to see this capital project move forward.
